analysis.one_liner: Opens Freedom of Information Act requests to the presidency, Congress, and federal courts.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it was referred to committee and a subcommittee in 1991 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Right now, the Freedom of Information Act lets citizens request documents from federal agencies, but the White House, Congress, and the courts are not covered. This bill would change the law's definition so the President, Vice President, their offices, the House, the Senate, and the federal courts' administrative office would all have to turn over records on request, just like agencies already must. The bill was introduced in November 1991 with no cosponsors and never advanced past a subcommittee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Any citizen, journalist, or watchdog group who wants to see what the government's most powerful branches are doing. Today they can demand records from executive agencies but not from the White House, the House or Senate, or the courts' administrative arm; this bill would close that gap.

how_it_helps.text: The bill rewrites the Freedom of Information Act's definition of 'agency' to include the Executive Office of the President, the President and Vice President themselves, and any executive establishment [S3].
It extends the same records-access obligation to the House of Representatives and the Senate, and to the Administrative Office of the United States Courts [S3].
The result is 'equal access': the same legal right to request government records from the most powerful branches that already applies to ordinary federal agencies [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The President, Vice President, members of Congress, and the federal courts' administrative office would bear new costs and obligations: they would need staff and systems to process public records requests, and some internal and deliberative documents could become public.
analysis.who_pays_short: The White House, Congress, and the courts

drawbacks.text: Covering the House and Senate under the Freedom of Information Act would expose internal congressional deliberations, and constituents' personal correspondence sent to members seeking casework help could be swept into public disclosure regimes that agencies' systems are built to handle but congressional offices are not [S3].

Applying the Act to the President and the Executive Office raises the concern long debated in open-government law that forced disclosure of presidential advice and decision-making records could chill candid internal deliberation, which is why separate presidential-records rules have historically existed [S3].
The bill was a single page with no procedures or transition rules for the new offices it covers, so even supporters would have had to work out how disclosure would function in practice [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — that the public should be able to request records from the presidency and Congress just as it can from agencies — is a real, broadly supported transparency principle. The bill's weakness was design, not principle: one short section, no carve-outs for personal constituent correspondence or deliberative material, no transition plan. A better-drafted version would have answered those objections; this one gave opponents nothing to work with.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in November 1991, referred to the House Government Operations Committee and then to one of its subcommittees, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Glenn English of Oklahoma introduced the bill on November 22, 1991 [S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Government Operations [S5].
Six days later it was referred further to the Subcommittee on Government Information, Justice and Agriculture, where it sat with no further action recorded [S5].
No cosponsors ever signed on [S4], and no committee or floor action of any kind followed before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The presidency, Congress, and the courts keep their exemption from public records requests, so the status quo for incumbent officeholders and the staff who guard their records was preserved at no cost.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbent officeholders in all three branches

for.name: Rep. Glenn English
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Government Operations
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never reported it out or held any recorded action on it.

against.name: Subcommittee on Government Information, Justice and Agriculture
against.role: Subcommittee of referral, House Government Operations
against.what_they_did: Received the bill six days after introduction and took no recorded action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so no partisan alignment on it was ever visible in the record.

industries.note: If enacted, the bill would have stripped these officeholders of their exemption from public records requests, exposing their internal documents to citizen scrutiny. The bill's death preserves their current shield from FOIA.

industries.industry: Records-management and legal services in government offices
industries.note: Covering the White House, Congress, and the courts under FOIA would have created work processing requests, but this is the ordinary cost of running a transparent government, not a private windfall.
